messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 46
- Gender: Non-binary
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Software Engineer
- Trauma Type: Police violence
- Pcl5: 54

Sam is a 46-year-old software engineer who came to therapy at their wife’s urging. They are South Asian, non-binary, and prefer they/them pronouns. Their story unfolds in fragments, like scattered lines of code that no longer compile into a coherent whole.

The event happened two years ago, on a Tuesday night in early November. Sam was driving home from the office after a late deployment, the highway nearly empty. A police cruiser’s lights flashed behind them. They pulled over immediately, hands at ten and two, heart already pounding. The officer approached, flashlight blinding, and ordered them out of the car. Before Sam could explain—they had done nothing wrong—they were on the ground, face pressed into cold asphalt, a knee grinding into their lower back. The officer accused them of matching a description: a suspect in a nearby robbery. Sam kept saying “I didn’t do anything,” but the words came out as gasps. The handcuffs were too tight. They remember the smell of rubber from the officer’s gloves and the sound of a second car pulling up, more boots on pavement. After thirty minutes, the officer let them go—no charges, no apology, just a gruff “You can leave.”

Sam didn’t tell anyone for weeks. They drove home that night, showered, and sat on the edge of the bed, awake until dawn. At work the next day, they opened their IDE and stared at a screen of blue syntax. A coworker tapped their shoulder, and Sam flinched so hard they knocked over a coffee mug. They apologized, said they were tired.

Now, in sessions, Sam describes the aftermath in precise, segmented sentences, like comments in a script. They stopped driving on that highway. Then they stopped driving at all after dark. Then they stopped driving alone. Their wife now does most errands, and Sam takes public transit or works from home, though the train platform triggers a similar feeling—the scan for uniforms, the internal cortisol spike when someone moves quickly.

At work, Sam’s performance has slipped. They were once the lead for a critical API migration; now they avoid stand-up meetings where they have to speak, afraid others will see their shaking hands. They’ve noticed that certain sounds—a door slamming, a chair scraping—make their chest tighten. They wear hoodies with the hood up even in the office, a kind of armor. When a manager scheduled a video call with a client who works for a policing technology firm, Sam immediately emailed back with a vague excuse about a scheduling conflict. They lied. Avoidance is automatic now, a reflex.

Marriage has become strained. Their wife, Priya, is patient, but she sometimes sighs when Sam asks her to drive them to a grocery store four blocks away. Sam knows they are a burden. They wake most nights at 3 a.m., drenched in sweat, heart racing from a dream where the asphalt is wet and the officer’s knee is a full body weight. They don’t always tell Priya, because then she will worry, and that worry feels like another weight.

Sam has also noticed a shift in how they see the world. Before the stop, they believed that if they worked hard enough, followed the rules, kept their head down, they would be safe. Now they know that safety is a privilege they don’t have. They scan every patrol car from a distance. They plan routes to avoid police stations. They flinch when a siren wails, even on TV.

In the last session, Sam said, “I used to love driving at night. The highway was my thinking space. Now it’s a trap.” They looked at their hands, then back at me. “I don’t know how to get that back.”

They are still showing up to work, still writing code, still making dinner with Priya most evenings. But underneath it all, the stop is a permanent background process, consuming memory, slowing everything down.
